claims.text: Solidified FeNiCrMn undergoes a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent switch in its dominant deformation mechanism.
Dislocation glide dominates FeNiCrMn deformation at elevated temperatures and low strain rates.
Twinning-mediated plasticity dominates FeNiCrMn deformation at lower temperatures and high strain rates.
The proposed deformation-mechanism switch preserves the alloy's strength–ductility balance.
The controlled study uses homogenized, single-phase, Co-free FeNiCrMn with controlled grain size and minimal preexisting defects.
Temperature and strain rate are varied while alloy chemistry and initial microstructure are held constant.
Both tensile and compression loading are used to test the proposed response.
The relevant structural mediator is the relative activation and density of deformation twins versus slip bands and dislocation forests.
At lower temperatures and higher strain rates, insufficient thermal activation promotes deformation twinning.
Increased deformation twinning raises work-hardening capacity and supports simultaneous strength and ductility.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, enhanced thermal activation favors dislocation glide and dynamic recovery.
Dislocation glide and dynamic recovery at higher temperatures and lower strain rates reduce yield strength while increasing ductility.
High-rate, low-temperature testing will produce greater twin density, yield strength, and work-hardening rate.
Higher-temperature, lower-rate testing will produce lower twin density and yield strength but greater ductility.
Ambient quasi-static tensile testing provides the standard strength–ductility baseline for solidified FeNiCrMn.
The proposed transition may not apply when significant secondary phases, different processing histories, or compositional changes are present.
Dynamic studies of related high-entropy alloys indirectly support the expected transition between twinning and slip-mediated plasticity.

The mechanism-switch hypothesis would be falsified by an absence of condition-dependent microstructural variation or by failure of mechanical-property trends to correlate with the predicted microstructural changes.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as homogenized after solidification, whereas the boundary describes the applicable material as as-solidified. Homogenization generally makes the tested condition distinct from a strictly as-solidified state.
